Transorbital surgery - a game changer

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
43 year old Prof Darlene Lubbe is now recognised as the leading world expert in transorbital surgery. And over the last three years Groot Schuur hospital has done more of these operations than anywhere else in the world. it was standing room only last week when Prof Lubbe addressed the world's leading neurosurgeons in Europe.. She is the first ever to do this operation on a sphenoid wing meningioma, a tumour situated several centremers behind the eye and which leads to blindness.. Surgoens have to cut away the skull, and shift the brain to get to the tumour. This often puts pressure on the optic nerve leading to blindness. 1000's of SA's have this condition but doctors are loathe to cut away some of the skull ,. These cranitomies and the sugery that follows often lead to severe complications. So these ops are not performed which means that patients go blind. . Also recuperation is very very long. Now Dr Lubbe goes in through 8 pathways around the eyes and two in the nose.

Summary:
Her story starts 4 years ago, when she attended a medical conference and she saw a leading USA doctor perform transorbital procedures on a gadiva. But the doctor only spoke about the possibilities of this type of surgery and minor procedures that could be done. The Prof came back and shared her excitement with top SA neurosurgeon Prof Allan Taylor, who was initially sceptical and onthamologist Dr Hamzah Mustak. They trio spend 100's of hours working on gadivas and the operations began - not only did the team save patients from hectic surgery (cutting half the skull away) but in most instances patient's eye sight was saved. Recovery time - 3 days only. She also designed and developed, working in tandem with a top German instrument maker) a set of specialised instruments which have also just been introduced. She has also written a book with visuals for surgeons to learn the procedures.

Further information:
There are several other operations that can be performed through the nose and eye. Dr Lubbe is planning her next operation next THU or FRI. She will get permission for us to film.

SA and Groot Schuur and Prof Lubbe is leading the way. We have tons of videos, and pics. And for good measure, this Prof has been called on a few times to do transorbital surgery on dogs and even horses!!!

Press Release:


Brain surgery is one of the most common operations for tumours, where skilled surgeons have to cut bone from the skull to be able to operate. It’s a complex and dangerous surgery with long recovery periods and high risk of complications. Now a team of South African surgeons have developed a surgical technique that’s changing lives. Through the eye sockets and nostrils to some parts of the brain – that’s how specialists are now performing these complex surgeries. Carte Blanche explores this remarkable innovation.

Script:


Trans orbital Eye Surgery – Script

Its Sunday and she is finding some quiet time in a coffee shop to finish an article for a medical journal. Capetonian Professor Darlene Lubbe is fast becoming one of the world’s most innovative ear, nose and throat surgeons. A few days later her expertise will save the eyesight Ruwayda Cornelius, a 46-year-old mother of 3 who has a sphenoid wing meningioma. A benign tumor, behind one eye. severely impacting and damaging her optic nerve.

Ruwayda Interview: Its very blurry, its constantly wet and I can’t see far with it and its a lot of pain.

Professor Lubbe will be joined in the operation to remove her tumor will be ophthalmologist Dr Hamzah Mustak and Neurosurgeon professor Allan Taylor. Normally a patient like Ruwayda would undergo a craniotomy. Professor Taylor has done 100’s of them

Prof Taylor interview: I always say to patients, no body wants an operation on their head and nobody wants an operation anywhere close to the brain. We have to open the skull and work past or next to the brain in order to get to the eye so we are always open to finding new and smaller ways of doing things.

Ruwayda will not have to endure a craniotomy, which has a long recovery period - Instead her tumor will be removed by operating though her nostrils and eye sockets!

LINK: Quietly almost under the radar, a dedicated team of specialists here at Groote Schuur hospital have been performing a revolutionary new procedure, its call trans orbital endoscopic surgery and its going to be a game changer.

Extensively trained in endoscopic skull based surgery both here and abroad, Prof Lubbe is pioneering` this new surgery in south Africa and now around the world.

Question Derek: There was a demonstration in Europe that seems to have changed the course of your career?
Interview Prof Lubbe: I went to a world conference on endoscopic surgery of the brain and the skull and saw Chris Moe He is a professor at Washington university and he demonstrated this new technique where we made these incisions in essentially the four corners of the eye, four pathways that he described,

Here are the pathways he discovered using the eye sockets and nostrils.

Interview Prof Lubbe: and fascinated with this I came back and I teamed up with Hamzah Mustak, an ophthalmologist and I said we have to really look at this.


Prof Lubbe and Dr Mustak spend many hours practicing on cadavers in the morgue to see how far they could steer their instruments through the canals around the eyes.

Interview Dr Mustak: My main function was sort of to make sure that whatever we were attempting was safe to the eye the structures that are vital to sort of the eye.

They were surprised at the relative ease they could reach areas of the brain. Next they had to convince their colleague Professor Allan Taylor.

Interview Prof Taylor: My colleagues know me as a natural sceptic so I don’t jump into things easily. but I was confident that Darlene knew exactly what she was doing so I agreed to come in and have a look and the moment I saw it I recognized that this is something new and worthwhile.

The worlds first trans orbital sphenoid wing meningioma operation took place at Groote schuur three years ago and it was a success. But working conditions were cramped and there were no specialist instruments for this complicated procedure.

Interview Prof Lubbe: For this surgery to be reproducible and to be performed elsewhere in the world you need to it to be a two-person surgery and not three-person surgery.

So the Professor in conjunction with a leading German instrument maker Karl stolz designed a specialized set of instruments that were multi-functional.

LINK: Many of the instruments being used by the trio to operate on ruwayda today have been specially designed at Groote schuur. In fact, they going to be called the lubbe trans orbital endoscopic set.

It was a full house in the operating theatre as several doctors from the various disciplines came to observe the operation.

First incisions are made on the inside corner of the eyes and the upper eyelid. Because the tumor was compressing the optic nerve the team had to drill away the bone around it to free it up. Then they went through the outer part of the eye socket to remove different parts of the tumor. A GPS system steered them through the skull to show the exact location of the instruments relative to the brain lining. After more drilling, the tumor has been removed.

What has excited the medical team is that most patients vision has improved after the operation Its most likely because the team has been able to remove pressure from the optic nerve, something rarely achieved by traditional craniotomies.

Interview Prof Lubbe - So what we found then that actually our patients, all of them except 2 that were completely blind for a long time, had better vision.
Derek: Had improved...?
Prof Lubbe: Had improved vision.

Interview Dr Mustak: To be honest with you it was a great feeling from our side because its the ophthalmologist that the patient first present to. The fact that you could save vision or even in some cases improve vision in condition in which the outcomes were traditionally poor was really fantastic.

Caroline Murray's eyesight has also improved. She underwent a grueling craniotomy over two years ago to have her tumor removed. That operation wasn’t a success.

Interview Caroline Murray: They weren’t able to get too close to the cranial nerve and other vital parts of the brain so then they suggested that the next thing I needed to do was radiation because it hadn’t been removed completely.

This is an x-ray showing her tumor, still present after her craniotomy. Radiation did not help. She lost all sight in one eye. She was then referred to Prof Lubbe who performed trans orbital surgery and got most of the tumor out. Her recovery process was quick.

Interview Caroline Murray: the next day I was sitting on the balcony after surgery and I wondered if I could order a gin and tonic. That was how I felt, I really felt so good.

Best of all her eye sight had dramatically improved.

Interview Caroline Murray: By in large its good and I’m back on my motorbike, back on my bicycle and really leading a very good normal life.

To date there have been over 80 trans orbital endoscopic surgeries performed at Groote schuur. But its not only some brain tumors that can be removed with this approach. The team has removed eye tumors, cystic lesions and managed patients with thyroid eye disease.

LINK: It seems that the professor never stops working. She already has 4 other instruments awaiting patents and she has difficulty saying no to anybody. Even when there is a distress call from a vet.

Meet Vermintino, daughter of a south African champ filly Promise from my heart of the Varsfontein stud. She was born with a cleft palate.

Interview VET: ITs a condition that is quite difficult to fix in horses because of the length of the skull and the accessibility to that part of the anatomy.

Normally such horses have to be euthanized because of complications. Dr Deon van Tonder sent out a distress call to professor Lubbe, who assembled a team. And in a marathon 5-hour session, they fixed the cleft palate.

Interview Prof Lubbe: This horse survived and the vet showed me a picture a year later, sent me a picture with the horse now being pregnant, so that was a success story.

if the professor is not operating or writing for medical journals she is lecturing locally and worldwide. Professor Heinz Stammberger, is recognised as the world leader in endoscopic sinus and skull based surgery and seen here operating at the Graz university in Austria. He is following professor Lubbe's career with keen interest.

Interview Prof Stammberger: Not only I think, I’m convinced that what she is doing will and has already established herself as the leading figure in that field world wide I should add. and she is in the middle of developing an enormous skill and she is really pushing the frontiers.

Meanwhile the team is quick to deflect glory.

Derek Question: Even after years of surgery was it exciting to be at this operation being performed for the first time?
Interview Prof Taylor: In surgery we are always a little hesitant to call things first and I don’t think that should be the aim right to do something first or to do the most of something. That’s not important, what’s important is developing something that is going g to help patients in the future.

The specialists now work together like a well oiled machine.

Interview Dr Mustak: By operating more frequently with each other, we have sort of gotten to know each other so you can often preempt what the other one wants to do or where the other one wants to be so we can coordinate the effort.
Interview Prof Lubbe: We've got at Groote schuur access to all the latest instrumentation so its been a fascinating journey learning about the other disciplines and how we can learn from each other and what we can do together.

Patients here and around the world like Ruwayda Cornelius will benefit from this team’s journey. 8 days after her operation Ruwayada was out and about and spending time with relatives.

Interview Ruwayda: I’m feeling fine, no more headaches, no big scar, most of all, my eyesight is coming back.
